details:
**Mexican Revolution (Emiliano Zapata and Pancho Villa)**
The decade-long revolution of the 1910s that overthrew dictator Porfirio Diaz. Peasant leader Emiliano Zapata of Morelos issued the 1911 Plan of Ayala demanding land redistribution and turned against President Francisco Madero; Zapata was later assassinated on the orders of Venustiano Carranza's government. Pancho Villa led revolutionary forces in the north.

**Ten Tragic Days (Decena Tragica)**
The 1913 coup in Mexico City that overthrew and led to the killing of President Francisco Madero. U.S. ambassador Henry Lane Wilson backed the plotters through the Pact of the Embassy. Pedro Lascurain served as president for less than an hour so the transfer of power to General Victoriano Huerta would look legal.

**Zimmermann Telegram**
A 1917 secret message from German foreign minister Arthur Zimmermann, decoded by British naval intelligence in Room 40, proposing a German-Mexican alliance against the U.S. in World War I. It promised Mexico the return of territory like Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona; President Carranza rejected it and kept Mexico neutral.

**Tampico Affair and the occupation of Veracruz**
In 1914, U.S. sailors were briefly arrested in Tampico, and Mexico's refusal to give a 21-gun salute as an apology led the U.S. to occupy the port of Veracruz. The occupation also aimed to stop the German ship SS Ypiranga from delivering arms to Huerta. The ABC Powers (Argentina, Brazil, and Chile) then mediated at the Niagara Falls peace conference.

**Punitive Expedition**
The 1916–1917 U.S. military campaign led by General John J. Pershing into northern Mexico to capture Pancho Villa after Villa raided Columbus, New Mexico. President Venustiano Carranza opposed the incursion, and Villa was never caught.

**Assassination of Leon Trotsky**
The exiled Soviet revolutionary lived in Mexico City, where he survived an attack led by the muralist David Alfaro Siqueiros in 1940. Later that year he was killed with an ice axe by NKVD agent Ramon Mercader, in a plot code-named Operation Duck. His bodyguard Robert Sheldon Harte died after the earlier raid.

**Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and el dedazo**
The party that ruled Mexico without interruption from 1929 to 2000, emerging out of the Maximato period dominated by Plutarco Elias Calles. Under "el dedazo" ("the big finger"), the outgoing president personally chose his successor. Its rule ended with the 2000 election victory of the National Action Party (PAN) candidate Vicente Fox.

**Battle of Puebla and the French intervention**
After President Benito Juarez suspended foreign debt payments for two years following the Reform War, France invaded. Mexican forces defeated General Charles de Lorencez at Puebla on May 5, 1862, now celebrated as Cinco de Mayo. Napoleon III then installed the Austrian Maximilian I as emperor, who was executed by firing squad at the Hill of the Bells in 1867, a scene painted by Edouard Manet.

**Pastry War**
An 1838–1839 conflict in which France blockaded and attacked Mexico over unpaid damages to French citizens, including a French pastry cook whose shop in Mexico City had been looted. Santa Anna lost a leg fighting the French at Veracruz.

**Tlatelolco Massacre**
On October 2, 1968, government forces, including the Olympia Battalion, opened fire on student protesters in the Plaza of the Three Cultures in Mexico City, killing many. It happened days before Mexico City hosted the 1968 Summer Olympics, under President Gustavo Diaz Ordaz.

**Lazaro Cardenas and oil nationalization**
In 1938, President Cardenas invoked Article 27 of the 1917 Constitution to nationalize foreign oil companies, creating Pemex and prompting an international boycott. In the same year, Mexico was the only country to formally protest the Anschluss to the League of Nations.

**Aztecs and Tenochtitlan**
The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and was centered on the Templo Mayor; Mexico City now stands on its ruins. The Aztecs farmed on chinampas, artificial "floating gardens," and fought ritual "Flower Wars" to capture prisoners for sacrifice. Hernan Cortes conquered the city in 1521.

**Olmec colossal heads**
The Olmec, Mesoamerica's earliest major civilization, lived on Mexico's Gulf Coast and carved giant basalt heads, thought to depict rulers. They are also known for jaguar figures.

**Porfirio Diaz and the cientificos**
Diaz ruled Mexico for most of 1876–1911, a period called the Porfiriato, guided by technocratic advisors called the cientificos, such as finance minister Jose Limantour. His 1908 interview with journalist James Creelman, in which he said Mexico was ready for democracy, helped inspire the opposition that set off the Revolution.

**Santa Anna and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo**
Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna dominated Mexican politics in the mid-1800s and lost Texas in 1836. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War and gave California and much of the Southwest to the United States.

**Bracero program and Operation Wetback**
The bracero program (1942–1964) brought Mexican laborers to work temporarily on U.S. farms. The 1954 U.S. deportation campaign known as Operation Wetback sent many Mexican workers back to Mexico.
